openers.phanerozoic-eon: The Phanerozoic is the eon of visible animal life, and it begins with a burrow. A rock section at Fortune Head, Newfoundland, marks its base, traced worldwide by the first Treptichnus pedum burrows. From about 538.8 Ma, complex life diversified suddenly and produced the first members of most modern animal phyla. Seas rose, continents collided, and the chemistry of the ocean swung between oxygen-rich and oxygen-starved. Everything that follows, from trilobites to the present, belongs to this one eon.
openers.paleozoic-era: The Paleozoic, the era of ancient life, opens at the same burrowed layer as the Phanerozoic itself. In its first period, sea level began a long, gradual rise, and shallow seas crept over the continents. Tiny mineral tubes, spicules and plates, often only millimetres long, record the first animals to build hard parts. Mountains rose on Gondwana's western margin while the Kalahari and Mawson cratons joined to complete its south. This era carries life from the first shelly seafloor to the eve of the dinosaurs.
openers.cambrian-period: Few stretches of time changed life as much as the Cambrian. Beginning about 538.8 Ma, animals diversified suddenly, and the first members of most modern phyla appeared. An asteroid about 1 km across struck what is now Estonia, and the first known footprints on land date to about 530 Ma. Under the seafloor, carbon and pyrite were buried in waters short of oxygen, and the chemistry of the sea rose and fell with each pulse. The period is the stage on which the animal kingdom took its modern shape.
openers.terreneuvian-epoch: The Terreneuvian is the Cambrian's first epoch, named for Newfoundland, where Fortune Head marks its base. Its rocks hold small shelly fossils, mineralized tubes and plates, in a nearly continuous record. Gondwana completed its southern half as the Kalahari and Mawson cratons met. Carbon and sulphur isotopes trace pulses of oxygen that spread from the deep ocean into shallow seas. Around 529 Ma a carbon spike and two new molluscs mark the epoch's first internal boundary.
openers.cambrian-series-2-epoch: Trilobites define this epoch: their body fossils first appear around 521 Ma, with exoskeletons of calcite. Radiodonts, the giant predators of the Cambrian, and eocrinoid echinoderms join them. China's Maotianshan Shales preserve an extremely diverse fauna, soft tissues and all, and among them the earliest known vertebrates. Mountains rose in Antarctica and South Australia. The epoch ends in crisis: the Sinsk Event, the Phanerozoic's first mass extinction, removed over 60% of animal species.

reviews.ediacaran-period: The Ediacaran opens on a limestone cap above the last snowball and closes with a mass extinction. In between, the Pan-African collisions built Gondwana, the Iapetus Ocean opened, and enough oxygen gathered to form an ozone layer. Life answered. The Avalon explosion produced large, soft-bodied fronds and tubes, the first trails crossed microbial mats, and Cloudina built some of the first mineral skeletons. Then, about 538.8 Ma, the Ediacaran biota and the shelled Cloudina vanished abruptly, and Cambrian animals spread into the empty niches.
reviews.terreneuvian-epoch: The Terreneuvian shows the Cambrian explosion getting started. A burrow trace, Treptichnus pedum, marks its base, and small shelly fossils record animals building hard parts in a rapid but orderly sequence. Pulses of oxygen spread into shallow seas and match the radiation of these shelly animals. Meanwhile seas rose over flat continents, Gondwana completed its assembly, and archaeocyath sponges built the first animal reefs. By its close, Sirius Passet in Greenland was preserving whole communities of soft-bodied animals.

prot-112.title: The Sturtian: fifty-seven million years of ice
prot-112.text:
Ice at or below sea level, on a continent near the equator: that is the evidence that the Sturtian glaciation was global. It lasted from about 717 to 660 Ma, some 57 million years. It was the first of the Cryogenian's great ice ages and the longest and most severe known glaciation after the Huronian. The supercontinent Rodinia then straddled the equator, yet its glaciers reached the shore.

The cold arrived only 0.9–1.6 million years after {{ref:prot-110}} erupted. One explanation joins the two: weathering of fresh basalt pulled carbon dioxide from the air, while Rodinia's breakup left mid-ocean ridges releasing little of it. In the snowball episodes, ice may have covered all but the highest mountains, with average temperatures near −50 °C.

How far the ice reached is still debated. It may have been a Snowball Earth, with ice at very low latitudes. It may instead have been several regional glaciations, or a slushball with open water at the equator. That the glaciation happened is not in dispute.

prot-111.title: Snowball Earth: did the whole planet freeze
prot-111.text:
Glacial deposits laid down in the tropics turn up on every continent. Glaciers once reached sea level near the equator. From this comes the Snowball Earth hypothesis: that Earth's surface froze nearly completely, most often linked to the Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations of the Cryogenian.

Not everyone accepts the full freeze. The glaciation itself is accepted, but scientists still dispute whether ice covered the whole planet or left a slushball, with an open band of water around the equator. Either way, life struggled. Thick ice blocking sunlight would have severely hindered primary production, the growth of algae and other organisms that make food from light, in shallow seas.

The trigger is thought to lie in Rodinia's breakup. The same breakup is linked to the rapid evolution of the Ediacaran and Cambrian. The frozen world sits right before the great burst of complex life.

prot-122.title: Beardmore mountains rise in Antarctica
prot-122.text: A supercontinent's pieces began drifting home. From about 633 to 620 Ma, the Beardmore orogeny, a mountain-building episode, raised ranges in Antarctica. It reflects the final breakup of Rodinia. As that supercontinent came apart, its fragments started moving back together, toward a new assembly called Pannotia.

prot-137.title: The Shuram excursion, carbon's biggest swing
prot-137.text:
The largest negative carbon-13 excursion in Earth's history took 50 million years to recover. The Shuram excursion is a shift in the ratio of carbon-13 to carbon-12 in Ediacaran rocks, first noticed in South Australia's Wonoka Formation. Its timing is debated: it began around 573 Ma and ended around 562 or 551 Ma. Diagenesis, chemical change after burial, may exaggerate it.

No one knows what caused it. The oxygen-using Ediacaran biota radiated during it, apparently exploiting a surplus of oxidants. It may have helped spark the rise of animals that led to the Cambrian explosion.

prot-143.title: White Sea and Ediacara Hills: crowded sea floors
prot-143.text: One bed on Russia's White Sea coast holds the highest diversity of Ediacaran fossils found, with real ecological complexity. The White Sea biota flourished from 560 to 550 Ma. In South Australia lie the Ediacara Hills, the type locality that names the period. They preserve abundant fossils of about 555 Ma, like a community of the same age in Sonora, Mexico.

prot-147.title: Cloudina builds the first animal skeletons
prot-147.text:
Holes drilled through tiny tubes prove that something was hunting by the late Ediacaran. The tubes belonged to Cloudina, one of the cloudinids, an early animal family that lived about 550 Ma. Cloudina, Namacalathus and a dozen other organisms built mineralized tubes in carbonate rocks 549–542 Ma. They are among the earliest and most abundant small shelly fossils with mineral skeletons.

Why build a skeleton then? Rising oxygen lowered ocean acidity and raised seawater calcium around the Ediacaran–Cambrian boundary, which may have prompted it. Predatory borings are common in Cloudina tubes, so predation was at least present. The cloudinids died out at the base of the Cambrian.

prot-150.title: The Proto-Tethys Ocean opens
prot-150.text: The Proto-Tethys Ocean lasted from the latest Ediacaran to the Carboniferous, about 550–330 Ma. It lay between Baltica and Laurentia to the north and Gondwana to the south. After the Cadomian events, it formed the eastern part of an ocean system that was sinking, or subducting, beneath Gondwana's northern margin.

prot-151.title: A supermountain feeds the Cambrian explosion
prot-151.text:
A mountain range more than 8,000 km long and 1,000 km wide rose as the East African Orogeny raised the Transgondwanan Supermountain. Erosion tore it down. Its debris built the Gondwana Super-fan, over 100 million km³ of sediment laid down over 260 million years.

That flood of sediment coincided with the Cambrian explosion and probably helped early animals diversify. By the Ordovician, the great range had been worn down to a plain in what is now Ethiopia.

prot-149.title: Nama: the thin last chapter of the Ediacaran
prot-149.text: By the end of the Ediacaran, no more than a dozen of 92 possible modes of life were occupied. The Nama assemblage, the last Ediacaran biotic interval, about 550–539 Ma, was depauperate, short of species. It never regained the diversity lost as the White Sea biota gave way. Namibia's Nama Group sites preserve Rangea, erniettomorphs and true animals from shallow seas shaped by tides, storms and deltas.

prot-148.title: The Malagasy orogeny: India joins Africa
prot-148.text: India rammed into Africa in the Malagasy orogeny, a collision that ran from the Ediacaran into the Cambrian. It struck a block already joined from Azania and the Congo–Tanzania–Bangweulu Block. The collision deformed Madagascar, eastern East Africa and southern India about 550–515 Ma, adding another seam to assembling Gondwana.

prot-153.title: The Baykonurian, a late Ediacaran ice age
prot-153.text: Ice returned late in the Ediacaran. The Baykonurian glaciation lasted from around 547 to 540 Ma. Its deposits occur in Asia and Africa, and it apparently affected both hemispheres. It has been proposed as one contributor to the Cambrian explosion that followed.

prot-154.title: Trail-makers grow longer and sense farther
prot-154.text: By the terminal Ediacaran, the animals that left trails had bodies over eight times longer than wide. They grew steadily more elongate. Their trails formed tighter, more accurate loops, and around 540 Ma their sensory range grew from millimetres or centimetres to decimetres. Some of the behavioral and sensory novelties credited to the Cambrian may therefore have begun in the last stretch of the Ediacaran.

prot-155.title: The Southern Oklahoma Aulacogen floods with magma
prot-155.text: Roughly 250,000 km³ of magma spread over about 40,000 km² of what is now Oklahoma. The Southern Oklahoma Aulacogen, a failed arm of a continental rift, formed between 525 and 550 Ma as Laurentia split. Its other two arms became spreading zones of the young Iapetus Ocean. Its flood basalts began or peaked around 540 Ma and are linked to an end-Ediacaran event. The magma came in two phases, first gabbro and then rhyolite.

prot-156.title: The end-Ediacaran extinction clears the stage
prot-156.text:
Very few organisms crossed the line. The end-Ediacaran extinction, also called the Kotlin Crisis, is a mass extinction near the close of the Ediacaran, the last period of the Proterozoic.

It swept away the old world. Acritarch diversity fell sharply. The soft-bodied Ediacaran biota disappeared, and so did the shelled Cloudina and Namacalathus. Both groups vanish abruptly, at 538.8 ± 0.2 Ma. Because the soft and the shelled went together, their loss cannot simply reflect a closing window of preservation.

The chemistry of the sea shifted too. A major negative carbon-isotope excursion marks the boundary, and in Oman it coincides with the last Namacalathus and Cloudina. The survivors' descendants inherited an emptied world. Cambrian animals radiated into the vacant niches.

camb-001.title: Fortune Head: where the Cambrian begins
camb-001.text:
A burrow marks the start of the Cambrian. At Fortune Head, Newfoundland, a rock section serves as the formal base of the period, traced worldwide by the first Treptichnus pedum burrows. That trace fossil is linked to early priapulid worms. When finds turned up a few metres below the boundary, geologists began using its whole trace assemblage instead.

Modern radiometric dating puts the boundary at 538.8 ± 0.6 Ma; in 2022 the age was revised from 541 Ma. It opens the Paleozoic Era and the Phanerozoic Eon, and now lies below the first trilobites and small shelly fossils. Several chemical markers show a drastic change in the environment around this time.

camb-007.title: Orthid brachiopods open their shells
camb-007.text: Orthida, an order of brachiopods, shelled animals that look like clams but are not, appeared in the Early Cambrian, in the Botomian. They began to differentiate late in the Early Cambrian. By the late Cambrian they had diversified into many forms, 2–5 cm wide. In the shelf seas of the Ordovician they became very diverse.

camb-010.title: Small shelly fossils: the first hard parts
camb-010.text:
Most are only millimetres long: mineralized tubes, spicules and plates. These small shelly fossils form a nearly continuous record from the latest Ediacaran to the end of the Early Cambrian. Graham Budd's scheme divides them into worlds. A Tube world ran from 550 to 536 Ma; a Sclerite world of halkieriids, tommotiids and hyoliths ended about 525 Ma.

The record matters because it is fairly continuous. It shows phyla appearing in a rapid but orderly sequence, not a sudden jumble. Marks of selective predator attacks suggest predation helped drive new species. Most were thought wiped out in the end-Botomian extinction, but their apparent disappearance may partly reflect the loss of phosphate preservation.

camb-004.title: The Cambrian sea rises over the continents
camb-004.text:
As the Cambrian began, the sea started to rise, and it kept rising gradually through the whole period. This marine transgression was the second-greatest sustained sea-level rise of the Phanerozoic, driven as the climate grew warmer.

Shallow seas spread across flat, eroded surfaces such as the sub-Cambrian peneplain and the Great Unconformity, burying them under marine sediments. Water covered Baltica and much of Antarctica, and marine invertebrates flourished in the shallows. In North America this Sauk transgression began in earnest only in the middle Cambrian.

camb-013.title: The Neugrund impact strikes Estonia
camb-013.text: Around 535 Ma, an asteroid about 1 km across struck what is now the Gulf of Finland, off Estonia. Accounts of the crater differ: the Cambrian page describes a complex crater about 20 km wide with inner ridges, while the Neugrund page gives 8 km. It was once dated to the Ordovician, around 470 Ma, before newer research gave it a Cambrian age.

camb-014.title: The Pampean orogeny builds Gondwana's western edge
camb-014.text: Long before the Andes, mountains rose on Gondwana's western margin. The Pampean orogeny built them between about 535 and 520 Ma. It partly involved an exotic terrane, a crustal block from elsewhere, that docked against Gondwana's proto-Pacific edge. A belt of its igneous rocks formed from 525 to 515 Ma.

camb-016.title: Cuyania breaks away from Laurentia
camb-016.text: Part of Argentina began life in North America. Around 530 Ma, a block called Cuyania rifted away from Laurentia's Ouachita embayment. The split opened a new ocean that kept widening into the Early Ordovician. Paleomagnetic evidence, the record of ancient magnetism in rocks, supports Cuyania's Laurentian origin. It later docked against Gondwana.

camb-017.title: First footprints on land
camb-017.text:
Could Cambrian animals walk out of the sea? The first known footprints on land date to about 530 Ma, though the evidence that arthropods were ashore so early is unconfirmed. Early Cambrian trace fossils suggest mollusc-like animals could spend at least 15 minutes out of water.

Later tracks are clearer. At the Cambrian–Ordovician boundary, about 490 Ma, large amphibious arthropods, perhaps euthycarcinoids, left trails across coastal dunes.

camb-018.title: Kuunga–Damara collisions complete Gondwana
camb-018.text:
Around 530 Ma the Kalahari and Mawson cratons met in the Kuunga–Damara orogeny, completing southern Gondwana. Collisions in East Antarctica's Lützow-Holm and Prydz belts climaxed at the same time. In the Damara orogeny, deformation and metamorphism peaked between 530 and 500 Ma.

The west took longer. A narrow ocean separated Amazonia from Gondwana until about 530 Ma. In the mid-Cambrian, Amazonia collided with the São Francisco–Congo and Río de la Plata blocks, stitching West Gondwana together along the Transbrasiliano lineament. The last stages of this assembly overlapped with the Cambrian explosion.

camb-020.title: A carbon spike and two molluscs mark Stage 2
camb-020.text: Geologists need markers they can find anywhere. Around 529 Ma, a positive carbon isotope excursion called the ZHUCE coincides with the first appearances of two molluscs, Watsonella crosbyi and Aldanella attleborensis. Together these markers reliably indicate the boundary between the Fortunian and Cambrian Stage 2.

camb-019.title: Oxygen pulses breathe life into Cambrian seas
camb-019.text:
The early Cambrian ocean breathed in and out. In Stages 2 and 3, linked carbon and sulphur isotope excursions record heavy burial of organic carbon and pyrite in productive seafloor waters short of oxygen. Burial locked away material that would otherwise use up oxygen. Oxygen-rich waters then spread from the deep ocean into shallow seas, extending the habitable seafloor.

Each pulse undid itself. Oxygenation cut burial rates, and anoxia returned; the cycle repeated several times. The pulses match the radiation of small shelly fossils and the Cambrian arthropod radiation isotope excursion, or CARE. Meanwhile, rising strontium ratios in seawater show stronger continental weathering, which fed nutrients to the oceans.

camb-022.title: Baltica collides with Arctida
camb-022.text: Between 528 and 510 Ma, Baltica and Arctida collided, and the Timanide Orogen rose where they met. The mountains did not last. Erosion of the belt began in the Cambrian and grew stronger in the Ordovician, shedding sediment as the range wore down.

camb-021.title: Ramgarh, an impact crater of uncertain age
camb-021.text: Somewhere between 528 and 395 Ma, an impact struck what is now Ramgarh in India. Uranium–lead dating gives that wide window. Other studies propose a younger age still. The crater is a reminder that not every event can be pinned to a date, and that some impacts of this era remain loosely placed in time.

camb-023.title: Archaeocyaths build the first animal reefs
camb-023.text: The oldest large structures built by animals were reefs of sponges. Archaeocyaths, cup-shaped sponges fixed to the seafloor with porous skeletons of lime, are first known from East Siberia at the start of the Tommotian, 525 Ma. With cyanobacteria, they built the reefs of the early Cambrian in warm tropical seas. They diversified rapidly in Stage 3, then declined sharply in Stage 4.

camb-025.title: Sirius Passet: a Cambrian window in Greenland
camb-025.text: In northern Greenland, Sirius Passet preserves a whole early Cambrian community. Part of the Buen Formation, dated about 523–518 Ma, it holds a fauna like that of China's Maotianshan Shales. Its animals were most likely preserved under a death mask of microbial mat that sealed them after death. With the Burgess Shale and the Maotianshan Shales, it ranks among the major Lagerstätten, sites of exceptional preservation, of the Cambrian.
